title: Whole Milk 1 gal

drivers.name: Price increase (5.1%)
drivers.evidence: Two past instances at $4.56: sales 195 (-11%) and 119 (-43%); noise-adjusted estimate for price hikes is -25%.

drivers.name: Store closure (Monday)
drivers.evidence: One day lost; historical closures reduce sales ~10% based on similar product behavior.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 207.6. The store closes Monday (1/7 of the week), reducing potential sales. A price increase to $4.56 (+5.1%) is expected to suppress demand. Past price hikes to $4.56 (2026-09-28, 2026-10-05) saw sales drop to 195 and 119—11% and 43% below baseline. The noise-adjusted effect of price increases is estimated at -25% (shrunk from observed -27% due to low frequency). The store closure reduces effective selling days by ~14%, but sales are not fully proportional; a conservative -10% impact is applied. No event or promotion drives uplift. The classical model’s 1.00 is overridden by known price and closure effects. Combined, median multiplier is shrunk toward 1.0 due to limited data.

brief:
PRODUCT: Whole Milk 1 gal | category Dairy | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-15 (5 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 4.56 (+5.1% vs regular price 4.34)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 207.6 | 5%-95%: 133.4 - 290.4 | 10%-90%: 156.2 - 281.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-22% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
